The only dhaba near the college in Sagar had four plastic tables, and Farhan's group took two every evening. Farhan, nineteen, always ordered first for Parul: plain dal, no onion, no garlic, roti kept away from the non-veg pan. He had learnt her Jain rules in the first week and never joked about them. His own Ammi's rule was halal only, so he stuck to paneer here.
One evening Deepak pulled his chair back when Ramu, the cleaner's son who studied with them, sat down. 'My family doesn't eat with—'
Farhan cut in, quietly. 'Parul's rule is about what's on her plate. Yours is about a person. That's different.'
Parul nodded and passed Ramu the pickle. Deepak looked away, but stayed.

In the shared kitchen of their residence in Cape Town, Diego, twenty, was making his grandmother's pozole for Sunday dinner, the way his family did every week back in Monterrey. Pork, of course. Then he remembered: Aisha ate halal, and Kiran was vegetarian. He split the pot, made a bean version on the side, and labelled both.
When Thabo came in to help, Lars muttered that Thabo's pan was 'dirty' because tripe had been cooked in it. Diego frowned. 'It's washed. If you don't eat tripe, fine. But a pan isn't dirty because of who used it.' Thabo shrugged, jaw tight.
That night eight people ate from two pots, and Diego handed Thabo the first bowl.

qa.q: Which dish was Diego making?
qa.a: His grandmother's pozole.

qa.q: What was Diego feeling when Lars called Thabo's pan dirty?
qa.a: Diego felt uncomfortable and annoyed at the unfairness, frowning because the remark was really about a person, not the food.

qa.q: What did Diego do well to respect everyone at the table?
qa.a: He split the pot into a pork and a bean version with labels so Aisha and Kiran could eat, and challenged the unfair remark about Thabo.

qa.q: How might Thabo have felt when Diego defended the pan and served Thabo first?
qa.a: Thabo probably felt respected and less alone after the hurtful remark, though the tight jaw shows it still stung.

"Jyoti, try my chicken?" Aditi pushed her plate across the mess table, then pulled it back. "Oh wait, sorry. Jain. I forgot."
"It's fine. I've got my dal." Jyoti smiled. "Thanks for remembering after."
Rekha sat down with her tray. "Can I have some of your pickle, Jyoti? Only if it's okay."
Jyoti hesitated for half a second. At home, Dadi would never let a cook from outside touch her jar. She said things about "those people" that Jyoti had never questioned.
"Of course," Jyoti said, and passed it over.
Walking back, Aditi asked, "You froze. Why?"
"My Dadi's rules. Some I keep, like no meat, no onion. Some..." Jyoti kicked a pebble. "Some I think are just unfair. About who can touch what."
"So which ones will you keep?"
"The ones about my plate. Not the ones about people."

passage:
I'm Hafsa, and last Diwali I learned how complicated one plate can be.

Tejas and I have eaten from the same mess tray for two years. He's vegetarian; I eat only halal. In the hostel we just work around it: I skip the meat curry when it isn't halal, he skips the eggs, and we share everything else.

So when he invited me home to Nashik for Diwali, I didn't think about food at all. His mother cooked a feast, all vegetarian, which I loved. But she served me on a separate steel plate kept on a high shelf, and later I saw her wash it apart from the others.

I felt it in my stomach, a small cold drop.

On the train back I told Tejas. He went red. "I didn't know she still did that. It's not right. I'll talk to her."

I told him I'm happy to eat vegetarian in his home forever. The separate plate is the part I can't pretend not to see.

qa.q: How long have Hafsa and Tejas eaten from the same mess tray?
qa.a: They have eaten from the same mess tray for two years.

qa.q: What did Hafsa feel on seeing the plate washed apart?
qa.a: Hafsa felt hurt, a small cold drop in the stomach, sensing a line drawn around the guest rather than the food.

qa.q: How does Hafsa separate a fair food rule from an unfair one?
qa.a: Hafsa gladly respects the family's vegetarian food but names the separate plate as the unfair part, and tells Tejas honestly.

qa.q: How does Tejas react when Hafsa tells him?
qa.a: Tejas is embarrassed, says it isn't right, and offers to talk to his mother.

passage:
Warden's note, Girls' Hostel Block C, 14 March

There was tension in the common kitchen this week. A first-year complained that Maria's beef fry was in the same fridge as her vegetarian tiffin and called it "disgusting". Maria cried.

Hafsa, a second-year who is fasting for Ramzan, came to me the same evening with a plan: separate labelled shelves by diet, lids on everything, and one rule written at the top: "Respect every restriction. Nobody's food is dirty."

She said, "I don't eat pork, and I'd hate it touching my food. But I'd hate even more being called disgusting."

What I did next: I put up her notice, sat the three of them down together, and asked the first-year to apologise for the word, not the preference. She did. On Friday, Maria waited until sunset to eat so she could break the fast with Hafsa.

qa.q: What rule was written at the top of Hafsa's plan?
qa.a: Respect every restriction. Nobody's food is dirty.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's comment about being called disgusting suggest she feels?
qa.a: Hafsa feels protective and a bit indignant; she understands food limits but finds calling someone's food disgusting far more hurtful.

qa.q: Why was the warden's response fair to everyone?
qa.a: It kept each person's restriction with labelled shelves and lids, while asking for an apology for the insulting word, not the preference.

qa.q: What was it like for Maria when Hafsa stepped in?
qa.a: Maria, who had cried, likely felt supported, and showed it by waiting until sunset to eat with Hafsa.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a hostel helping housemates respect each other's food restrictions while rejecting the idea that anyone's food is dirty.

Thursday, hostel, late
Irfan brought his mother's biryani back from Hyderabad today and offered me some. I'm vegetarian, he knows, so he'd kept a separate box of veg biryani just for me. That's the kind of friend he is. We ate on his bed with Marcus and Ramesh.
Then Mummy called. When I told her, she said, "Don't eat from the same boxes as those boys. And keep your own plate." I just said "okay" and hung up. I felt sick, and angry. Irfan had cooked for me, well, his mother had. What does "those boys" even mean?
Here's what I've decided. I'll stay vegetarian, because I actually believe in it. I'll respect Irfan not eating pork, which Ramesh keeps forgetting. But I'm not going to act like my friends are dirty. I'll talk to Mummy properly when I'm home at Diwali, not on the phone.
Chetan

qa.a: A separate box of veg biryani.

qa.a: Chetan felt sick and angry, because the call treated a caring friend as someone to keep apart from.

qa.a: Irfan would probably feel hurt and insulted, after making sure Chetan had a vegetarian box.
